title: Chronic Conditions as a Potential Explanation for the Cognitive Advantage of Immigrant Older Adults: Evidence from the Health and Retirement
content: Background: Immigrants in the United States have been observed to experience slower cognitive decline than U.S.-born individuals. While this cognitive advantage may partly reflect the positive health selection of those who migrate, it remains unclear whether differences in physical and mental health conditions explain these disparities in cognitive aging. Objective: To examine whether lower prevalence of cardiometabolic conditions (diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and body mass index) and depressive symptoms help explain the association between immigration status and cognitive decline among middle-aged and older adults in the United States. Methods: This study used longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults aged 50 and older. Cognitive function was measured at multiple time points across waves. Immigration status (immigrant vs. U.S.-born) was the primary independent variable. Cardiometabolic conditions and depressive symptoms were tested as potential mediators. Linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate cognitive decline over time, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was conducted to examine mediation pathways. Results: Immigrant individuals experienced significantly slower cognitive decline than U.S.-born individuals. This advantage was partially explained by a lower prevalence of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, high body mass index, and depressive symptoms among immigrant individuals. However, immigration status remained a significant predictor of cognitive decline even after accounting for these mediators. Conclusions: The cognitive advantage observed in immigrant individuals appears to be partially explained by more favorable cardiometabolic and mental health profiles. These findings provide support for the healthy immigrant effect and suggest that physical and mental health differences may contribute to variations in cognitive aging by immigration status.
